settings.title: What shapes cloud projects for London businesses
settings.body: Cloud migrations for London businesses tend to be constrained less by the technology than by the building, the lease and the calendar. The pattern repeats often enough to plan around.

items.q: Serviced offices remove control of the connection
items.a: In multi-tenant and serviced buildings you rarely control the incoming line, the contention ratio or the risers. That argues for cloud-first services, cellular failover and a design that does not assume the landlord’s network behaves.

items.q: Lease events are the real migration deadline
items.a: A move or a lease break is usually what forces the decision, which compresses the timeline and makes sequencing matter. Migrating before the move, rather than during it, avoids doing two difficult things in the same week.

items.q: Hybrid working is the default, not the exception
items.a: London teams split the week between office, home and client sites more than most. That pushes identity, conditional access and device management to the front of the design rather than treating them as a later phase.

settings.title: Small configuration decisions can have long-term consequences
settings.body:
Technology settings are often changed little by little as businesses evolve. A new employee needs additional access, a cloud service is introduced, security policies are adjusted or a supplier makes changes during a project. Individually these updates seem minor, but over time they can leave systems configured in ways that no longer reflect how the business operates.

Configuration issues rarely appear after a single change. More often, they develop after years of updates made by different IT providers, software vendors and internal teams. Everything continues working, yet the organisation is carrying unnecessary operational and cyber security risk without realising it.

Reviews examine how your systems are actually configured against how they were intended to be, and the output is a prioritised remediation list rather than a raw scan dump. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled.

settings.title: Most exposed passwords were never stolen from you
settings.body: The credentials that put a business at risk usually leak somewhere else entirely. A member of staff signs up to a supplier portal, a forum or a retail site with their work email address and a password they also use at work. That third party is breached, and the pair ends up in a list traded between criminals. Nothing was compromised on your network, and nothing on your network can tell you it happened.

items.q: Breach dumps, combolists and stealer logs
items.a: Older breach dumps are the least urgent, because the password has often been changed and the hash may be slow to crack. Combolists are aggregated email and password pairs assembled for credential stuffing, which is why password reuse is the whole problem. The one that deserves immediate attention is an infostealer log, taken from a machine infected with malware that harvested everything the browser had saved along with active session cookies. Those cookies can let someone resume a signed-in session without ever needing the password or the second factor.

items.q: A match is not the same as a breach
items.a: An alert tells you a credential appeared in a dataset, not that anyone has used it. The triage questions are whether the password is still current, whether that account has multi-factor authentication, whether the same password protects anything else, and whether the source suggests a compromised device rather than a third-party leak. Answering those turns a frightening notification into a short, specific job. Treating every match as an emergency is how teams start ignoring the alerts.

items.q: Why monitoring is detection, not prevention
items.a: We would rather be straight about this. Monitoring cannot remove your data from anywhere, and no supplier can, whatever they imply. What it buys you is time between the exposure and someone trying it, which is the window in which a reset costs you ten minutes instead of an incident. It works because it sits alongside the controls that actually block the attempt: multi-factor authentication, a password manager so reuse stops being tempting, and conditional access rules that make an unexpected sign-in harder to complete.

settings.title: The first hour matters more than the report
settings.body:
Plenty of services will send you a monthly PDF listing exposures. That is a record, not a response. What changes the outcome is what happens in the hour after a credential surfaces, and whether anyone is on the hook for doing it.

In practice that means resetting the affected password and any account sharing it, revoking active sessions and tokens rather than only changing the password, checking the mailbox for forwarding rules or filing rules that should not be there, and confirming multi-factor is enrolled and enforced on that account. Where the source looks like an infostealer log, the device itself is treated as compromised and taken out of use until it has been rebuilt, because rotating a password on an infected machine simply hands over the new one.

We handle those steps with you rather than emailing a list and leaving it. If you want the controls that reduce how often this happens at all, password management and awareness training do most of that work, and managed detection and response covers what happens if someone does get in.

tabs.label: Trusted services
tabs.html: A genuine SharePoint or Dropbox share notification, sent from the real platform, pointing at a document that happens to be malicious. Because the notification really did come from the platform, it passes every check a filter can reasonably make.

tabs.label: QR codes
tabs.html: A QR code in an attachment, because it moves the attack onto a phone where there is no filtering and no visible address bar. The message itself carries no link for anything to inspect.

tabs.label: Thread hijacking
tabs.html: A reply inserted into an email thread that has been running for weeks, from a supplier whose mailbox was compromised last month, so it has real history above it. Nothing about the conversation looks new or unusual.

tabs.label: MFA interception
tabs.html: The one that catches the most people. An attacker with a stolen password sits between you and Microsoft using a proxy page that looks exactly right. You type the code, and they capture the session token rather than the password. Multi-factor authentication still matters enormously, but on its own it is not the finish line people assume.

tabs.label: Where filtering stops
tabs.html: Filtering deals with volume. What it will not do is make a convincing message from a real supplier account look wrong, which is why authentication, monitoring and a team that knows to check unusual requests all sit alongside it.

settings.title: The expensive one involves no malware at all
settings.body: The most costly email attacks we deal with do not carry a payload. Someone gets into a mailbox with a working password, sits quietly and reads. They learn how your invoices are worded, who signs things off, when your finance person is on holiday. Then they send one message asking for bank details to be updated, from a real internal account, in the house style.

items.q: Why nothing gets flagged
items.a: There is nothing for antivirus to find, because nothing was installed. The usual tell is a mailbox rule the attacker added to hide their tracks, quietly moving replies into an obscure folder so the real owner never sees the conversation happening in their name. That is why alerting on new forwarding and filing rules matters more than it sounds.

items.q: The control that actually stops it
items.a: The other half of the answer is not technical. Any request to change bank details gets verified on a phone number you already had, never one supplied in the email itself. It is a dull control that defeats a very profitable attack.

settings.title: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, without the jargon
settings.body: Three records that decide whether anyone can send email pretending to be you.

cards.title: SPF
cards.text: Lists the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. If a message arrives from somewhere not on the list, the receiver has grounds to be suspicious. It breaks quietly when you add a new sending tool, such as a mailing platform or a booking system, and nobody updates the record.

cards.title: DKIM
cards.text: Signs your outgoing mail cryptographically so the receiver can confirm it genuinely came from you and was not altered on the way. It answers the question SPF cannot, which is whether the message itself is authentic rather than just the route it took.

cards.title: DMARC
cards.text: Ties the two together and tells receivers what to do when a message fails. This is where most businesses stop too early. A DMARC record set to none is monitoring only, and does nothing to stop spoofing. Moving carefully to quarantine and then reject is what actually protects your domain, and it is exactly what we manage for you.

settings.title: Antivirus asks one question
settings.body: Have I seen this file before? That question works right up until an attacker uses something it has not seen, or does not use a file at all.

items.q: Attacks that carry no malware at all
items.a: Someone gets hold of a working username and password, often from a convincing phishing page, and simply logs in. Nothing has to be installed, so nothing gets flagged. From there the attacker uses tools that are already on the machine, which is why this approach is known as living off the land. To antivirus it all looks like normal admin work.

items.q: Why behaviour beats signatures
items.a: MDR looks at behaviour instead of file signatures. It is less interested in what a file is called and more interested in what is happening: an account signing in from two countries an hour apart, a process quietly turning off protection, files being encrypted in bulk, a workstation suddenly scanning the rest of the network. Those patterns are hard to disguise, because they are the attack itself rather than the tooling used to deliver it.

During working hours, when the security tooling raises an alert it creates a ticket in our helpdesk. A small team cannot staff three shifts properly, and pretending otherwise means alerts sit unread overnight, which is exactly when ransomware tends to run. Being straight about the split matters more than sounding impressive, and it is easy for you to verify.

settings.title: What a SIEM is actually for
settings.body: A SIEM does something quite specific: it gathers logs from everywhere, puts them into a common format, and looks for patterns across them that no single system could ever see on its own.

items.q: Three boring events, one attack
items.a: Your firewall records a connection from an unfamiliar country. Microsoft 365 records a successful sign-in for a finance account. An endpoint records a script running out of a temporary folder. Individually each one is unremarkable and would never justify waking anybody. In sequence, within nine minutes, they describe an attack in progress.

items.q: Having logs is not using them
items.a: Correlation is the difference between having logs and being able to use them. Most businesses already produce all the evidence they need and simply have it scattered across six consoles that nobody compares, each retained for a different length of time, several of which quietly overwrite themselves.

settings.title: How this differs from MDR, and who is watching
settings.body: These two get sold interchangeably and they are not the same thing. Managed detection and response is focused: it watches endpoints and identities for behaviour that looks like an attack and acts to contain it. SIEM and SOC is wide: it collects from everything, correlates across sources, keeps the history, and gives you the evidence trail. Most businesses start with MDR because it stops incidents. SIEM earns its place when you need to see across the whole estate, or you have compliance and audit obligations to satisfy.

settings.title: How a managed Mac fleet actually works
settings.body: Most Mac problems in a business are not really Mac problems. They are the result of nobody managing the devices centrally.

cards.title: Zero-touch setup
cards.text: With Apple Business Manager and automated device enrolment, a Mac bought for a new starter can be shipped straight to them. It enrols itself the first time it is switched on, applies your settings, installs the apps they need and lands ready to work. Nobody has to sit and build it, and nobody has to post it to us first.

cards.title: Settings that stick
cards.text: Configuration profiles let us set the things that matter once and have them hold across every device: full-disk encryption on, the firewall enabled, a sensible screen lock, and administrator rights given deliberately rather than by default. New Macs inherit the same standard automatically.

cards.title: Updates and offboarding
cards.text: macOS releases, browsers and business apps are kept current on a schedule instead of whenever someone gets round to clicking the prompt. When a device is lost, or someone leaves, it can be locked or wiped remotely and the licences reclaimed rather than quietly disappearing.

settings.title: Mixed environments break on identity, not hardware
settings.body: Hardly any business runs on one platform only. Designers and developers want Macs, finance and operations are on Windows, and the two have to share the same files, the same email and the same security rules. When that goes wrong, it is almost never because the hardware cannot cope. It is because identity and file access were never joined up.

items.q: Start with identity
items.a: The fix is to stop treating Macs as visitors on the network. Connect them to the same directory everyone else uses, so a Mac user signs in with the same Microsoft 365 account, the same multi-factor authentication applies, and revoking access when someone leaves genuinely revokes it everywhere.

items.q: Files, printing and the awkward bits
items.a: Keep shared files in SharePoint and OneDrive rather than a legacy file share, which is where cross-platform setups usually start to creak. Then test the practical things on both platforms instead of assuming they work. Printing, VPN and conditional access are the usual culprits.

items.q: Handled by us, not a reseller chain
items.a: We are a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so the Microsoft 365 and Entra ID side is handled directly by us rather than through a reseller chain, and the Mac side is managed to the same standard as the PCs beside it.

settings.title: Macs are not exempt
settings.body: The idea that Macs do not get malware is comfortably out of date. macOS is actively targeted, most commonly by information stealers dressed up as legitimate installers or browser downloads, which go after saved passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets. The delivery method is usually a person being persuaded to run something, which is exactly why endpoint protection and user awareness both matter.

items.q: What macOS already does for you
items.a: macOS does ship with some solid defences of its own. Gatekeeper and notarisation check what is allowed to run, XProtect removes known malicious software, and System Integrity Protection stops much of the operating system being tampered with. Those are a solid floor, not a managed security programme. None of them tell you that a device has stopped receiving updates, that encryption was switched off, or that someone has been granted admin rights they should not have.

items.q: Cyber Essentials applies to Macs too
items.a: The five Cyber Essentials controls apply to Macs exactly as they apply to Windows: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. We hold Cyber Essentials certification ourselves and take clients through it, and Macs are assessed alongside everything else rather than quietly left out of scope.

settings.title: What we account for in Birmingham
settings.body: Birmingham pairs a dense professional-services core around Colmore Row with a manufacturing and engineering supply chain spread across the wider West Midlands. Those two halves of the city want very different things from IT, and a business often sits in both at once.

items.q: City-centre professional firms, multi-floor and multi-tenant
items.a: Serviced and multi-tenant buildings in the business district rarely let you touch the incoming connection or the risers. That pushes the design towards resilient wireless, cellular failover and cloud-first services rather than anything that assumes control of the building’s infrastructure.

items.q: Supply-chain security requirements arrive from customers
items.a: Firms supplying automotive and aerospace primes increasingly find Cyber Essentials or an equivalent written into purchase terms. The certification itself is straightforward; the awkward part is usually the unsupported machine or shared login that has to be dealt with first.

items.q: Sites across the conurbation, not one address
items.a: Operations often run across Birmingham, Solihull and the Black Country, which makes consistency the real problem: the same policies, the same patch state and the same support route at every location, rather than three arrangements that grew separately.

items.q: Within reasonable reach for onsite work

items.q: Sustained construction and relocation activity
items.a: Large-scale infrastructure and development work across the city has kept commercial relocation unusually frequent. Moves are where IT most often goes wrong, and the recurring cause is connectivity lead times booked too late rather than anything technical.

items.q: Several sites should still mean one identity
items.a: Operating across the conurbation often means each location grew its own arrangements, with separate logins, separate file stores and separate ways of doing things. Consolidating to a single identity per person, with access granted by role, removes most of the friction people feel when they move between sites and removes the accounts that accumulate when someone changes location. It also makes leavers a single action rather than a checklist per building.

items.q: Project sites open and close, and IT has to match
items.a: Where work runs on a project basis, sites appear for a period and then stand down. Treating connectivity, hardware and access as something to set up and recover repeatedly, with a standard build rather than a bespoke one each time, keeps mobilisation quick and stops equipment quietly disappearing at the end of a job. The cost of a standard kit list is recovered the second time it is used.

items.q: Budgets that expect the spend to be defensible

items.q: Production and office IT sharing one network
items.a: In smaller manufacturers the office switch and the machine on the floor are frequently the same network, because it grew that way. Separating them is usually the single highest-value piece of work available, and it rarely requires new hardware.

items.q: Working across Bradford and Leeds as one business
items.a: Staff moving between sites in the same week need their files, phone extension and permissions to follow them. That is an identity and cloud question rather than a networking one, and it is cheaper to solve properly than to work around.

items.q: Onsite attendance is a planned journey, not a call-out
items.a: Our engineers are based in Stevenage and travel north, so a Bradford visit is arranged rather than immediate. In practice most faults are resolved remotely long before a visit would arrive, and we would rather be straight about the travel than describe ourselves as local.

items.q: Older building stock shapes what is physically possible
items.a: Much of Bradford’s commercial space is in converted mill and older industrial buildings, where thick stone walls, long cable runs and limited riser access constrain what a network can do. Wireless surveys in these buildings routinely produce different answers from the floorplan, and cabling work is often the unglamorous prerequisite to everything else.

items.q: Machines usually outlive the software that drives them
items.a: A press or a production line bought fifteen years ago is often still perfectly serviceable, and still controlled by a PC running something no longer supported. Replacing the machine to solve a software problem is not a sensible answer. Isolating that PC on its own network segment, removing its need for internet access, and backing up its configuration is the pragmatic one. The goal is that an unsupported system cannot be reached from the office network and cannot reach anything else.

items.q: Backups that only cover the office miss the production data
items.a: Office files are usually protected because they live in a cloud platform somebody manages. Production data frequently is not: machine configurations, job files, quality records and the small local database on the shop floor PC that nobody thinks of as a server. Those are the things that make a rebuild slow when hardware fails. Listing what a full recovery would actually require, then checking each item is covered, is a job worth doing once and reviewing yearly.

items.q: Welsh language is a configuration requirement, not a preference
items.a: Organisations delivering public-facing services in Wales may have obligations to offer Welsh alongside English. In IT terms that reaches into templates, signatures, forms, website content and sometimes keyboard and locale settings. It is far easier to build in at setup than to retrofit across a live estate.

items.q: Public-sector adjacency raises the assurance bar
items.a: Suppliers to Welsh public bodies are often asked to evidence security controls in a formal questionnaire rather than a conversation. Having documented answers on access control, retention and incident response ready in advance saves weeks on a tender.

items.q: Media production moves large files on deadlines
items.a: Video and audio work generates volumes that ordinary office broadband and ordinary backup windows were not sized for. The practical answers are staged local storage, sensible sync rules and being honest about what a connection can actually carry.

items.a: Engineers travel from London and Stevenage, so a Cardiff visit is planned rather than immediate. We would rather state that plainly than list a virtual Cardiff address and imply otherwise. Remote resolution handles most of what arises, and we plan onsite work around genuine need.

items.q: Operating either side of the border
items.a: Businesses based in Cardiff frequently trade across England and Wales, which can mean two sets of public-sector frameworks, procurement portals and language expectations to satisfy from a single IT estate. Designing for both at the outset avoids maintaining two half-solutions.

items.q: Broadcast and production deadlines narrow the change window
items.a: When output is scheduled, maintenance cannot simply happen on a convenient evening. Work has to fit around transmission and delivery commitments, which means agreeing windows in advance and having a tested way back if a change misbehaves. The alternative, deferring everything until it is urgent, is how organisations end up doing risky work at the worst possible moment.

items.q: Contributors who are not employees still need access
items.a: Production work brings in freelancers, contributors and post houses who need particular material for a defined period. Handling that through named, time-limited access to specific content, rather than broad shares or files passed around, keeps control of the material and makes it possible to say precisely who could reach what. It is also markedly easier than trying to recall a link that has already been forwarded.

items.q: City-centre growth means frequent moves and fit-outs

items.q: Retention is a records decision before it is a storage one
items.a: Regulated firms carry obligations about how long client records are kept and how they are produced if asked. That is a policy question, but it lands as a technology one: retention rules on mailboxes and document libraries, a legal hold that survives an employee leaving, and a search that can actually find everything on a matter. settings.title: How to choose an IT support company in London

items.q: Ask what “fast response” actually means
items.a: A response commitment is only meaningful if it is stated in hours or working days and applies to a defined priority level. Ask for the priority framework and the committed response time at each level, and ask what proportion of issues are resolved on first contact.

items.q: Ask where the engineers are actually based
items.a: A London address does not always mean staffed premises in London, and plenty of providers list a registered or serviced office. items.a: Certifications are checkable, so check them. Cyber Essentials certificates are listed on the IASME certified organisation register, and Microsoft partner status can be confirmed through Microsoft. Be wary of unverifiable claims such as “award-winning” with no named award, or ISO certification that is stated but not evidenced.

items.q: Ask who you will actually speak to
items.a: For a business of five to a hundred and thirty people, the difference between a named team who know your setup and a rotating first-line queue shows up the first time something breaks. Ask how many people will handle your account and whether the service desk is UK-based.

items.q: Ask what leaving looks like

settings.title: Two numbers decide everything

tabs.label: RPO: work you can lose
tabs.html: How much work can you afford to lose? That is your recovery point objective. If backups run nightly, your RPO is up to 24 hours, which means a failure at four in the afternoon costs you the whole day. For a finance team mid month that might be genuinely serious. For other work it is an annoyance. Only you can say which.

tabs.label: RTO: time you can be down
tabs.html: How long can you be down? That is your recovery time objective. Restoring a large fileserver from cloud storage is not quick, and if the honest answer is two days while the business needs four hours, no amount of backup software fixes that. The design has to change instead, usually towards replication or standby systems for the handful of things that genuinely cannot wait.

tabs.label: Why both come first
tabs.html: Get those two numbers agreed and everything else follows from them. Skip them and you end up with backups that technically exist and a recovery that takes a week, which is the situation most businesses are quietly in.

settings.title: Your backup is a target, not a safety net
settings.body: Ransomware crews worked out years ago that encrypting live data is only half a job. If the victim can restore, they do not pay. So the backups get attacked first, and the tools people rely on most are the ones sitting on the same network with the same administrator credentials.

items.q: Keep one copy beyond reach
items.a: At least one copy has to be somewhere the attacker cannot touch. Immutable storage that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, separate credentials that are not the ones your domain admin uses daily, and multi-factor authentication on the backup console itself. The old three copies, two media, one offsite rule still holds up, with the modern addition that one copy should be genuinely unchangeable.

items.q: Retention is a security decision
items.a: Attackers commonly sit inside a network for weeks before triggering anything. If your retention is short, your clean restore point may already have been deleted by the time you need it. Retention is a security decision, not just a storage cost.

settings.title: Microsoft 365 is not backing up your data
settings.body: This one catches out well-run businesses regularly. Microsoft keeps your service running and protects its own infrastructure. It does not keep a point-in-time copy of your data for you to roll back to, and its own shared responsibility model says so plainly.

items.q: Why retention policies are not backups
items.a: Retention policies, litigation hold and the recycle bin help within limited windows, and none of them give you what you actually want at the worst moment, which is the ability to say put this mailbox, or this SharePoint site, back exactly as it was on Tuesday morning. Deleted items age out. A user with permissions can destroy a lot of shared content quickly, and ransomware syncing through OneDrive will happily do the same.

items.q: What actually closes the gap
items.a: The fix is unglamorous and cheap relative to the risk: an independent backup of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, held separately from the platform itself, with retention you have actually chosen rather than inherited.

settings.eyebrow: What drifts if nobody owns it
settings.title: A tenant does not stay tidy on its own
settings.body: Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace are set up once, usually carefully, and then reality happens. People join and leave, someone shares a folder to get a job done on a Friday, a trial licence quietly becomes a renewal, an app gets granted access and is never looked at again. None of it is negligence. It is what a live system does when no one has been given the job of tending it.

items.q: Leavers who never fully left
items.a: Offboarding usually gets the obvious part right, which is disabling the sign-in. What tends to survive is everything attached to that person: files owned by their account, a shared mailbox they still have rights to, an app password issued years ago, a personal device still enrolled. The tidy version archives the mailbox, transfers ownership of their files to a named colleague, revokes tokens and sessions rather than only the password, and then releases the licence. Done in that order, nothing is lost and nothing is left open.

items.q: Licences bought for a headcount you no longer have
items.a: The common pattern is paying for more seats than people, while some of the people you do have sit on a licence tier above what their role needs, and a handful sit below what they actually use. Reviewing assignment against real usage two or three times a year usually pays for the review several times over. As a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider we can adjust your licensing directly rather than sending you to a portal to work it out yourself.

items.q: Sharing links that outlived their purpose
items.a: Anyone-with-the-link sharing is genuinely useful and genuinely hard to retire, because the link keeps working long after the project ends and nobody remembers creating it. Expiry dates on external shares, a periodic report of what is shared outside the business, and a default that favours named access over open links keep this manageable without making collaboration painful.

items.q: Third-party apps holding standing consent
items.a: Someone signs in to a tool with their work account and grants it permission to read mail or files. That consent persists whether or not the tool is still in use, and it is not visible unless somebody looks. Reviewing granted permissions and deciding whether users can consent on their own behalf is a small piece of configuration that closes a route people rarely think about.

settings.title: Available is not the same as backed up
settings.body:
Both Microsoft and Google are explicit that they guarantee the availability of the service, not the recoverability of your content. Their job is that the platform is there; keeping a copy of what you put in it is yours. Deleted items sit in a recycle bin for a limited window and then go, and a compromised account that deletes deliberately can empty that bin too.

So part of managing a tenant is making sure something independent is holding a copy, and that somebody has actually restored from it. A backup nobody has tested is a belief rather than a control. We cover that with Microsoft 365 backup and Google Workspace backup, and the wider recovery picture sits in business continuity and disaster recovery.

The rest is unglamorous and matters: multi-factor enforced rather than merely available, conditional access rules that fit how your team actually works, admin accounts separated from everyday accounts, and someone reading the alerts. That is the day-to-day of cloud management, and it is mostly invisible when it is being done properly.

settings.title: How long a migration really takes
settings.body:
For around 50 users, budget roughly seven days of actual configuration work from us. Here is where that time goes.

Seven days is the configuration effort, not the calendar. A 50 user move typically spans two to three weeks end to end, because the bulk copy runs in the background and the pilot needs a few days of real use before the rest follow.

cards.title: Discovery and readiness
cards.text: Before anything moves we find out what actually exists. How much mail and how many files, who owns the shared mailboxes nobody admits to using, which applications sign in with the old system, what state the devices are in. This is also where most nasty surprises get caught, while they are still cheap.

cards.title: Build and pilot
cards.text: We set up the new tenant properly, with security baselines, multi-factor authentication and licensing sorted from the start rather than retrofitted later. Then a small pilot group moves first. It is far better to find the awkward bits with four willing people than with all fifty at once.

cards.title: Bulk move and cutover
cards.text: Mail and files copy across in the background over several days while everyone carries on working in the old system. The switch itself is the short part, scheduled deliberately for a quiet window, followed by a few days of us being close by while people find the things only real use uncovers.

settings.title: Where migrations go wrong
settings.body: Moving mailboxes is the easy bit. Almost every migration that goes badly goes badly for the same handful of reasons, and none of them are the mail.

items.q: The things nobody owns
items.a: Shared mailboxes, distribution lists and meeting rooms get forgotten because no single person owns them, then reappear the morning after cutover when nobody can book anything.

items.q: Permissions and connected apps
items.a: Permissions on shared folders are assumed to carry over neatly and rarely do, so somebody either loses access to a folder they need or quietly gains access to one they should not have. Third party applications that authenticate against the old system stop working until each one is reconnected, and the list of them is always longer than anyone expects.

items.q: Phones, and the licences still billing
items.a: Everyone remembers the laptops. Half the workforce has mail on a phone that nobody has recorded anywhere, and if that is not handled they spend cutover morning locked out and irritated. Old licences are the last one, still quietly billing months later because nobody cancelled them.

items.q: None of it is difficult
items.a: It just has to be written down beforehand and worked through, which is precisely what the discovery stage is for.

settings.title: The move we get asked about most
settings.body: Google to Microsoft 365 has its own quirks, and they are worth knowing before you start rather than after. Google Docs, Sheets and Slides are not Office files. They convert on the way across, and anything with heavy formatting or a script behind it needs checking rather than assuming. Gmail labels are not folders either. A message can carry three labels at once, a folder structure cannot hold that idea, so decisions have to be made about what the mailbox looks like afterwards.

tabs.label: Drives & calendars

settings.title: The bin empties, and that is by design
settings.body: Google Workspace is genuinely resilient. Your data is replicated, the service stays up, and hardware failure is not something you need to think about. That is availability, and Google is clear that it is what they are responsible for. Retention is a different question, and the answer is a countdown rather than an archive.

items.q: Deletion is on a timer, not a shelf
items.a: Items removed from Gmail or Drive sit in trash for a limited period and are then purged. An administrator has a further short window to recover some of it, and after that the copy is gone rather than archived somewhere deeper. Most data loss we are called about is not dramatic: someone tidied a shared folder in good faith, and the discovery came weeks later when a colleague went looking for a file.

items.q: A departing employee takes their Drive with them
items.a: Files in a personal My Drive belong to that account. Suspend or delete the account without transferring ownership first and the files go with it, including anything they had shared with the team, which stops resolving for everyone else. Shared Drives avoid this because the team owns the content rather than an individual, but almost every business has years of work sitting in personal Drives regardless.

items.q: A compromised account deletes on purpose
items.a: Accidental deletion is recoverable within the window. Deliberate deletion by someone who has taken over an account is designed to defeat exactly that, and emptying the trash is part of it. This is the case that separates a backup from a retention policy: an independent copy sits outside the account, so nothing done inside it can reach the copy.

items.q: Ransomware reaches synced files
items.a: Drive for desktop keeps local and cloud copies in step, which is the point of it. If files are encrypted on the laptop, the sync does its job and carries the damage upward. Point-in-time restore is what gets you back to the state before the change, rather than trying to unpick which version of which file is intact.

settings.title: The test is the restore, not the backup
settings.body:
Backups fail quietly. They run, they report success, and the problem only shows up on the day someone needs a file back. That is why the measure worth caring about is whether a restore has actually been performed recently, not whether the job is green.

What we look for is granular recovery, so a single message or one folder can come back without restoring an entire account; coverage across Gmail, Drive, Shared Drives, Contacts and Calendar rather than mail alone; a retention period long enough that a deletion noticed months later is still recoverable; and a copy held independently of the Workspace tenant, so a compromise of the tenant cannot reach it.

Two practical questions are worth asking of any arrangement, including ours: how far back can you go, and how long would a realistic recovery take. If nobody can answer both, the position is not yet a backup. If you also run Microsoft, the same reasoning applies there and is covered by Microsoft 365 backup, with the broader plan in business continuity and disaster recovery.

settings.title: Full signal bars and unusable Wi-Fi are compatible
settings.body: A device showing four bars is reporting how loudly it can hear the access point, not whether it can hold a usable conversation with it. Most complaints about bad Wi-Fi come from environments with plenty of signal and too much interference, too many clients per radio, or access points shouting over each other.

items.q: Buildings defeat assumptions
items.a: Plasterboard is nearly transparent to Wi-Fi; concrete, foil-backed insulation, plant rooms, lift shafts and metal racking are not. Older buildings with thick walls and modern buildings with foil-lined insulation both cause problems, for opposite reasons. This is why a survey in the actual building beats a plan drawn from a floor plan.

items.q: More access points is a common way to make it worse
items.a: Adding units to fix a dead spot frequently degrades the whole floor, because neighbouring access points on overlapping channels interfere with each other. Correct channel planning and turning power down rather than up is usually what fixes a struggling network. Density needs designing, not increasing.

items.q: Guests, staff and devices should not share a network
items.a: A single shared network means a guest laptop sits alongside your file server and your card terminal. Separate networks for staff, guests and equipment such as printers, cameras and building systems keeps a compromised or simply infected visitor device away from everything that matters, and lets you apply different rules to each.

items.q: The shared password is the weak point
items.a: A pre-shared key known to every current and former member of staff cannot be revoked for one person, so in practice it never changes. Per-user authentication removes that problem entirely and means access ends when employment does, which is also the answer to the question an auditor will eventually ask.

settings.title: Design first, then install, then verify
settings.body:
A proper survey establishes what the building does to the signal, where the users and devices actually are, and what they are doing. The design that follows specifies access point positions, mounting, channel and power plan, and the cabling each position needs. Installing first and adjusting afterwards is how sites end up with equipment in the wrong places and no way to know why it is not working.

After installation the network is verified rather than assumed, walking the site to confirm real-world throughput and roaming behaviour. Wireless depends entirely on what is underneath it, so structured cabling and network monitoring are the two services most often specified alongside it.

settings.title: Having a firewall is not the same as being protected
settings.body: Almost every business we assess already owns a capable firewall. The box is rarely the issue. What it is running, and who last looked at it, usually is.

items.q: Firmware nobody wants to reboot
items.a: Firewall vulnerabilities get published, and because these devices sit on the public internet they are scanned and exploited quickly, sometimes within days of an advisory. An unpatched firewall is not a neutral risk, it is an internet-facing door with a known key. Yet firmware updates get deferred because nobody wants to reboot the internet during working hours, and then the deferral becomes permanent.

items.q: Rule drift
items.a: Somebody opened a port temporarily for a supplier in 2021 and it is still open. An any to any rule went in to get a project finished and never came out. Nobody can say which rules are still needed because there is no record of why they were added, so nobody dares remove any of them.

items.q: Expired subscriptions, silently
items.a: The intrusion prevention, web filtering and threat intelligence that make a next-generation firewall worth buying are licensed separately. When those lapse the device carries on passing traffic quite happily with its best features switched off, and nothing tells you.

settings.title: What next-generation actually means
settings.body: The phrase is on every vendor’s datasheet. These are the parts that earn it.

cards.title: Application awareness
cards.text: Older firewalls made decisions on ports. Modern traffic mostly rides over 443, so port rules tell you almost nothing. Application control identifies what is really passing through, which is how you allow a service you sanction while blocking one you do not, even though both look identical from the outside.

cards.title: Intrusion prevention
cards.text: Inspects traffic for known exploit patterns and blocks them in transit. It is one of the licensed features that quietly stops working when a subscription lapses, which is why we track renewals as part of the service rather than leaving it to a diary entry.

cards.title: Encrypted traffic inspection
cards.text: Most threats now arrive over encrypted connections, so a firewall that cannot look inside them is guessing. It is worth being straight about the trade-offs: inspection costs throughput, needs certificates deploying properly, and some traffic such as banking should be excluded deliberately. Done carelessly it breaks applications, which is why it is configured deliberately rather than switched on wholesale.

settings.title: VPN, or something better than VPN
settings.body: Traditional VPN does one thing: it puts a remote device on your network. That was fine when the alternative was nothing, and it is now the part of the setup attackers most want to reach, because one stolen laptop or one reused password buys them the whole internal network to explore.

items.q: Where remote access is heading
items.a: The direction of travel is access to specific applications rather than access to the network. A user is authenticated, their device is checked, and they are connected to the one system they need and nothing else. If that account is later compromised, the damage is bounded by design instead of by luck. Not every business needs to move immediately, but if your VPN currently drops everyone onto a flat internal network, that is worth revisiting.

items.q: What carries the weight today
items.a: Multi-factor authentication on VPN access without exception, accounts removed the day someone leaves rather than the following quarter, and internal segmentation so a compromised machine cannot reach your servers and your backups just because it is inside the building. We are a Fortinet partner and will recommend the right model for your size and connectivity rather than the box with the best margin.

settings.title: Catch problems before your team does
settings.body:
Most network outages give warning signs long before they bring things to a halt, if someone is watching. Without monitoring, the first you hear of a problem is when work stops.

WhizzIT provides continuous, proactive monitoring and management of your network infrastructure, with alerting, performance analytics and the hands-on management to act on what we see.

Monitoring runs continuously across your network hardware and connectivity, and alerts land in the same helpdesk queue our engineers already work to. WhizzIT is Cyber Essentials certified and a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so our security fundamentals are independently assessed rather than simply claimed. It is priced per user at a fixed monthly cost rather than bundled into rigid packages, so it scales with your team. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase.

settings.title: An alert nobody acts on is just a log entry
settings.body: Monitoring tools are easy to buy and easy to ignore. The difference between a dashboard and a service is whether an alert reaches a person who is expected to do something about it, within a time you have agreed. Everything else is decoration.

items.q: Thresholds tuned to the site, not to the vendor default
items.a: Out of the box, most monitoring alerts on values that mean nothing in your environment, and the team learns within a fortnight to dismiss them. Once that habit forms, the genuine alert is dismissed too. Tuning thresholds to what is normal for each device, and deliberately alerting on less, is what keeps the alerts worth reading.

items.q: The signals that actually precede an outage
items.a: Hardware rarely fails without warning. Rising interface errors on a switch port, a firewall session table filling steadily, a failing power supply in a resilient pair, disk latency creeping up, an access point rebooting nightly: each of these is visible days ahead if something is watching. That window is the entire argument for monitoring.

items.q: Capacity questions need history, not a snapshot
items.a: When someone asks whether the connection needs upgrading or whether the switch stack will cope with thirty more staff, the honest answer requires months of trend data. Monitoring that only shows the present moment can describe a problem but cannot support a purchase decision, which is where most of the budget conversations actually happen.

items.q: Knowing what is connected in the first place
items.a: Monitoring depends on an accurate inventory, and inventories drift. Devices get added during a project and never recorded, or replaced without the record being updated. Reconciling what is discovered on the network against what is documented is unglamorous and routinely finds equipment nobody had accounted for.

settings.title: Watching and fixing are different commitments
settings.body:
Plenty of arrangements notify you and stop there, which leaves the work exactly where it was. We act on what the monitoring shows: applying firmware updates in agreed windows, replacing hardware showing early failure, chasing the carrier when a circuit degrades, and reporting on what changed rather than only on what broke.

Monitoring the network is one layer. Security monitoring of endpoints and identity is a different discipline and is covered by managed detection and response, while the edge devices being watched here are configured and maintained under managed firewall.

settings.title: Connectivity you can count on
settings.body:
When your internet drops, so does your business, cloud apps, email, phones and card payments all rely on it. A single connection with no backup is a single point of failure.

WhizzIT sources and manages the right connectivity for each site, adds automatic failover, and uses SD-WAN to intelligently route traffic across links, so you get resilient, prioritised, always-on connectivity you don’t have to think about.

Connectivity is designed around how your sites actually communicate, then managed as one service rather than several separate supplier relationships. It is priced per user at a fixed monthly cost rather than bundled into rigid packages, so it scales with your team. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. settings.title: Two lines are not resilience if they share a duct
settings.body: Buying a second connection feels like buying resilience, and often is not. If both circuits run from the same exchange, along the same route, or terminate on the same piece of your equipment, one contractor with a digger takes out both. Diversity has to be designed rather than assumed.

items.q: Diverse carrier, diverse route, diverse hardware
items.a: Genuine resilience means the two services do not share a failure point: different providers where possible, physically different routes into the building, and separate terminating equipment. Where a truly diverse fixed route is not available at a site, 4G or 5G backup gives you a path that fails independently by definition, because it does not use the ground at all.

items.q: Failover that happens before anyone notices
items.a: The value is in how fast and how quietly the switch happens. A failover that drops every call and every session is better than an outage, but only just. SD-WAN monitors the health of each path continuously and moves traffic when a link degrades, not only when it dies completely, which matters because slow and lossy is more common than fully down.

items.q: Not all traffic deserves the same treatment
items.a: A voice call is ruined by 100ms of jitter that a file upload would never notice. Policy-based routing lets you put real-time traffic on the most stable path and bulk transfers on the cheaper one, and change that automatically when conditions shift. This is the part that a straight second line cannot do at all.

items.q: Bandwidth is rarely the actual problem
items.a: Most sites that feel slow are not short of bandwidth. They are suffering from contention at peak times, a saturated upload path, or one backup job running in business hours. Measuring before upgrading usually costs less than upgrading, and sometimes shows the circuit was never the constraint.

settings.title: Lead times decide project dates more often than budgets
settings.body:
New fixed circuits are quoted in weeks and occasionally months, particularly where a new fibre build or a wayleave from a landlord is involved. Anyone planning a move, a fit-out or a new site should start connectivity first and everything else around it, because it is the one element that cannot be compressed by working harder.

We source and manage the circuits rather than leaving you to hold the carrier relationship, so a fault is our call to make and chase. Connectivity sits alongside managed firewall at the network edge, and the monitoring that proves a link is degrading is covered by network monitoring.

settings.title: Get the foundations right
settings.body:
Everything on your network depends on the cabling underneath it. Poor or improvised cabling causes intermittent faults that are painful to diagnose and expensive to live with.

WhizzIT designs and installs structured cabling done properly, the right cable for the job, neat comms rooms, clear labelling and full testing and certification, so your network has a foundation you can rely on and easily extend.

Cabling is planned, installed and certified to standard, with the documentation handed over so future work does not start with guesswork. Everything runs through the same UK service desk that handles your day-to-day tickets, so there is no separate team to chase. items: Cat6, Cat6a and fibre optic cabling

settings.title: Intermittent problems usually start underneath
settings.body: Cabling faults rarely announce themselves. They surface as a call that drops once a day, a machine that negotiates at a tenth of its speed, or a camera that goes offline when the heating runs. Because the symptoms look like software, teams often spend weeks in the wrong place before anyone tests the cable.

items.q: Certification is not the same as it works today
items.a: A tester that lights up green confirms continuity. Certification measures the things that actually degrade performance: crosstalk, return loss, attenuation and length, against the standard for the category installed. It is also the only evidence that the installation met specification on the day, which matters when a fault appears two years later and nobody can agree what was installed.

items.q: Category choice is a decision about the next decade
items.a: Cabling outlives several generations of the equipment plugged into it, so the sensible question is not what today’s switches need but what the building will need before it is next refitted. The cost difference between categories is small next to the cost of pulling cable through an occupied building a second time.

items.q: Comms rooms fail for physical reasons
items.a: Heat, dust and improvisation account for a large share of hardware failures. A rack in a cupboard with no ventilation will shorten the life of everything in it, and a rack with no patching discipline turns a five-minute change into an afternoon. Ventilation, power, containment and labelling are not tidiness for its own sake; they decide how long a fault takes to find.

items.q: Labelling and records are the part that gets skipped
items.a: An unlabelled patch field means every future change begins with tracing. A documented schedule mapping outlet to patch panel to switch port turns that into a two-minute job. It is the cheapest thing to do during installation and the most expensive to reconstruct afterwards.

settings.title: The disruptive part is access, not the cable
settings.body:
Most of the work in an occupied building is about getting to places: ceilings, risers, and rooms that can only be entered outside business hours. Agreeing routes, containment and access windows before starting is what keeps an installation from becoming a series of interruptions, and it is the part most often underestimated when a date is promised.

New sites and fit-outs are considerably cheaper to cable before fit-out finishes than after, so this is worth raising early in any move. Cabling underpins everything else on the network, particularly business Wi-Fi, where access point positions dictate where outlets must land.
